gloss_terse: shut, close (of a well or pit)
gloss_readable: This rare verb appears only in Psalm 69:15, where the psalmist pleads that the mouth of the pit not close over him. The imagery evokes being swallowed alive by the earth or death itself. The Arabic cognate suggests bending or enclosing, which fits the visual picture of a well's opening shutting like a trap. The multilingual evidence (shut-, close-, fermer) confirms the spatial sense of enclosure.

senses.1: Used metaphorically of death or the grave closing over someone like the mouth of a pit shutting. The psalmist's plea in Psalm 69:15 draws on ancient Near Eastern imagery of Sheol as a devouring entity with gaping jaws. Cross-linguistic glosses emphasize the finality of closure, with Spanish cierre- and French fermer both carrying connotations of sealing off or trapping.

gloss_readable: A rare negative particle appearing only in Job 22:30. The text is difficult and may be corrupt, as BDB notes alternative readings proposing אֵל or אֱלֹהַּ instead. This form is common in Rabbinic Hebrew and Ethiopic as the ordinary negative, and appears in Phoenician inscriptions. The phrase אִי־נָקִי literally means 'the non-innocent,' though textual uncertainty surrounds the passage.

senses.1: Functions as a simple negative particle meaning 'not,' forming the compound אִי־נָקִי ('non-innocent') in Job 22:30. Cognate with Rabbinic and Ethiopic negatives, this rare form represents an archaic or dialectal variant. The Spanish al-no- and English 'not' reflect straightforward negation, though the textual corruption makes precise interpretation challenging.

gloss_terse: and I will be hostile to, treat as enemy
gloss_readable: In Exodus 23:22, God promises 'I will be an enemy to your enemies' within the covenant blessings. The root אָיַב means to be hostile toward or treat someone as an enemy. As a verb it's rare; the participial form אֹיֵב (enemy) is far more common throughout the Old Testament. The multilingual glosses preserve both the future tense and the relational hostility, capturing God's promise to take Israel's side against their foes.

senses.1: Divine promise of active hostility against Israel's enemies in the Covenant Code. The waw-consecutive perfect expresses future intent: God will engage in enmity on behalf of His people. Cross-linguistic renderings (and-I-will-be-enemy, seré-enemigo, Je-serai-ennemi) maintain the first-person commitment, emphasizing covenant solidarity. The parallel with צַרְתִּי (I will be adversary to) reinforces reciprocal divine protection.

gloss_readable: An interrogative adverb meaning 'where?' used in 2 Kings 6:13 when the king of Aram seeks to locate Elisha. This form appears in the Ketiv (written text) while the Qere (oral reading tradition) likely points to אֵיכָה. The question seeks spatial information, fitting the context where the king wants to know Elisha's location to capture him. Simple and direct across languages.

senses.1: Interrogative seeking spatial location. In 2 Kings 6:13, the Aramean king asks his servants where Elisha can be found, intending to send troops to seize him. The cross-linguistic evidence (where, dónde, où, wo) shows universal preservation of the locative question. The Qere/Ketiv variant suggests textual fluidity between related interrogative forms in Hebrew manuscripts.

gloss_readable: While אַיִל typically means 'ram,' it can also denote mighty or strong ones, particularly leaders or nobles. In 2 Kings 24:15, this construct plural refers to the elite of Judean society taken into Babylonian exile alongside King Jehoiachin. The term evokes strength and prominence, extended metaphorically from the powerful ram to powerful people. The bracketed glosses in translations suggest interpretive uncertainty about this rare usage.

senses.1: Metaphorical extension from 'ram' to human leaders and nobles, emphasizing their strength and prominence. In the deportation list of 2 Kings 24:15, these 'mighty ones' represent Judah's ruling class carried to Babylon. The Spanish fuertes (strong ones) and other translations' bracketing reveal the semantic shift from animal to human domain, leveraging the ram's symbolic power to describe societal elites.

gloss_readable: A rare Aramaic loanword meaning strength or help, appearing only in Psalm 88:4 in the phrase 'like a man who has no strength.' BDB notes the borrowing from Aramaic ܐܻܝܳܠܴܐ, distinguishing this from the more common Hebrew terms for strength. The psalmist describes himself as powerless, abandoned among the dead. The multilingual evidence clusters around force, strength, and help, reflecting physical and existential weakness.

senses.1: Denotes the absence of vital strength or capacity to act, used in Psalm 88:4 to describe the psalmist's utter helplessness. As an Aramaic loanword, it brings a nuanced sense of lacking vigorous life-force. The French force and Spanish fuerza emphasize physical power, while the context of being 'among the dead' suggests complete depletion. This rare term intensifies the lament's portrayal of human frailty before death.

gloss_readable: The feminine form of H0353 with first-person suffix, appearing in Psalm 22:19 where the psalmist cries 'O Lord, my help, hasten to my aid!' The parallelism with יהוה shows this term expressing desperate dependence on divine assistance. Like H0353, it's an Aramaic loanword, intensifying the plea for rescue. The multilingual glosses split between 'strength' and 'help,' both capturing the essence of needed empowerment.

senses.1: First-person cry for divine assistance in extremis. In Psalm 22:19's climactic plea, the psalmist identifies the Lord as 'my help' or 'my strength,' the only source of deliverance from mortal danger. The possessive suffix intensifies personal dependence. Spanish mi-fuerza and German mein-helfen diverge slightly between internal capacity and external aid, but both reflect the urgent need for intervention when surrounded by enemies and death.

gloss_terse: El-paran, place name (terebinth or palm of Paran)
gloss_readable: A geographical location at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, mentioned in Genesis 14:6 during the campaign of the eastern kings. The name means 'terebinth (or palm) of Paran,' and BDB identifies it with various forms: אֵלָה, אֵילַת, אֵילוֹת. Close to Ezion-geber, this was a strategic port town. The multilingual glosses preserve the composite name, with some translating 'El' as 'God' though it likely refers to a tree.

senses.1: Ancient harbor settlement near the wilderness of Paran, captured by Kedorlaomer's coalition in Genesis 14:6. The name's etymology suggests either a sacred terebinth tree or a prominent palm, marking this oasis location. Identified with later sites like Elath and Ezion-geber, it served as a key port on the Red Sea trade routes. French Dieu-Paran reflects possible theophoric interpretation, though botanical origin seems more likely.

gloss_terse: and is there not? (irregular negative with existential particle)
gloss_readable: An unusual construction in 1 Samuel 21:9, where David asks 'Is there not here a spear or sword?' The form is likely irregular for אֵין with pleonastic יֵשׁ, creating a double emphasis. Some scholars suggest dialectal influence from Aramaic אִין. The text shows syntactic compression where negation and existence collide. Translations struggle to capture the Hebraic emphatic denial turned into urgent question.

senses.1: Emphatic interrogative negation seeking urgent confirmation of availability. David's question in 1 Samuel 21:9 combines negative and existential particles for rhetorical force: 'Surely there is (something) here?' The Spanish y-no-hay and French est-là-pas attempt to preserve the double construction. This dialectal or colloquial form may reflect spoken Hebrew's flexibility with existential constructions, especially under duress as David flees from Saul.

gloss_terse: Iezer, personal name (abbreviated form of Abiezer)
gloss_readable: A Manassite clan name, the shortened form of Abiezer ('my father is help'). Numbers 26:30 uses this abbreviated version in the census list, while other texts employ the full form. Iezer was reckoned as a 'son' of Gilead in the tribal genealogies. The gentilics Iezerite and Abiezrite both appear in Scripture, showing fluid use of abbreviated and full name forms in ancient Israel.

senses.1: Clan designation within the tribe of Manasseh, representing descendants of Iezer/Abiezer. In Numbers 26:30's census, this shortened form appears without the theophoric element 'father,' though the meaning remains understood. The multilingual glosses simply transliterate, as typical for personal and clan names. This variant demonstrates Hebrew onomastic flexibility, where abbreviated forms functioned interchangeably with fuller theophoric names in genealogical contexts.

gloss_readable: The gentilic form with definite article, designating members of the Iezer/Abiezer clan within Manasseh. Numbers 26:30 uses this to denote the family group descended from Iezer. The article makes it definite: 'the Iezerite [family].' This grammatical form is typical in census and genealogical lists where clan membership needed clear articulation. Equal to אֲבִי הָעֶזְרִי in other passages.

senses.1: Definite gentilic referring to the Iezerite clan as a recognized family unit within Manasseh's tribal structure. The article הָ- specifies this particular group in Numbers 26:30's census list. Multilingual renderings (the-Iezerite, los-iezeritas, le-Iezerite, der-Iezerite) uniformly preserve the definiteness, indicating an established, identifiable kinship group. This contrasts with indefinite usage, emphasizing the clan's recognized standing in Israel's tribal confederation.

gloss_terse: and show yourselves firm, be strong (uncertain Hithpael form)
gloss_readable: A textually uncertain Hithpael imperative in Isaiah 46:8, where God calls transgressors to 'show yourselves firm' or 'act like men.' BDB notes multiple interpretations: the Targum, Jerome, and others derive it from a root meaning 'establish,' while Lagarde and Cheyne suggest reading from בּוֹשׁ (be ashamed) instead. Thesaurus even proposes denominative from אִישׁ (man). The multilingual evidence shows significant variation, with some bracketing it as uncertain.

senses.1: Imperative calling for firmness or resolve, possibly urging idolaters to strengthen themselves for confrontation with divine reality. Isaiah 46:8's context involves God challenging Israel to remember their rebellion and His uniqueness. The Spanish afianzaos (make yourselves firm) and English be-firm support the establishment reading. However, textual uncertainty and diverse conjectures show this rare Hithpael defied easy understanding even in ancient translations, leaving the precise nuance debated.

gloss_readable: A Manassite mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 7:18. The name means 'man of majesty' or 'man of splendor,' combining אִישׁ (man) with הוֹד (majesty/splendor). Such theophoric or descriptive names were common in Israelite onomastics, often expressing parental aspirations or divine attributes. The multilingual glosses simply transliterate since proper names resist translation.

senses.1: Personal designation for a member of Manasseh's genealogy in the Chronicler's expanded tribal records. The name's components (man + majesty) suggest hopeful naming at birth, perhaps acknowledging divine glory or anticipating the child's distinguished character. As a hapax legomenon in Chronicles' genealogical material, Ishhod receives no narrative development, functioning solely as a genealogical link. The bracketed glosses indicate transliterators' uncertainty about vocalization or textual tradition.

gloss_terse: the Ethanim, seventh month name (month of steady flows)
gloss_readable: The pre-exilic name for the seventh month (later Tishri), appearing in 1 Kings 8:2 during Solomon's temple dedication. The name derives from אֵיתָן meaning 'perennial' or 'ever-flowing,' likely referring to the steady wadis of autumn after summer drought. This was October-November, a time of reliable water flow before winter rains. The Assyrian month Ululu and Arabic أَيْلُول preserve cognate forms.

senses.1: Ancient Canaanite month designation marking the autumn season when streams returned to steady flow after summer's desiccation. In 1 Kings 8:2, Solomon times the temple dedication for this agriculturally significant month, the beginning of the civil year and season of harvest festivals. The definite article הָ- marks it as the recognized name. Cross-linguistic transliteration (Ethanim, Etanim) preserves the Hebrew form, though the underlying meaning ('perpetual flows') reveals agricultural-calendrical reasoning behind the nomenclature.

gloss_terse: and Accad, city name in Babylonia
gloss_readable: One of four cities constituting Nimrod's kingdom in Genesis 10:10, alongside Babel, Erech, and Calneh in the land of Shinar. Accad corresponds to the Babylonian Akkadi, mostly known as a land or district but also a city. Its precise location remains uncertain; it may be the city of Sargon I (Agade/Agane). This was the heartland of the Akkadian empire, giving its name to the Akkadian language and culture.

senses.1: Ancient Mesopotamian city in Nimrod's primeval kingdom, representing early post-Flood urbanization and imperial power. Genesis 10:10 lists it with Babel and other foundational cities in Shinar (southern Mesopotamia). The name survives in Akkadian, the great Semitic language that dominated cuneiform literature. Multilingual glosses (Accad, Akad, Akkad) show slight orthographic variation but maintain the historical-geographical referent to this cradle of Mesopotamian civilization.

gloss_terse: cruelty of, fierceness (abstract noun in construct)
gloss_readable: An abstract noun appearing only in Proverbs 27:4 in the phrase 'the cruelty of rage and the outpouring of anger.' The construct state connects אַכְזְרִיּוּת (cruelty, fierceness) with חֵמָה (rage), creating a genitive relationship. The verse asks rhetorically who can stand before jealousy, ranking it above even fierce wrath. The term derives from the root אכזר (to be cruel), emphasizing savage intensity.

senses.1: Denotes the savage, pitiless quality of intense anger in Proverbs 27:4's comparison of destructive emotions. Paired with 'outpouring of anger,' this construct phrase depicts wrath's merciless character, yet the verse subordinates both to jealousy's power. Spanish crueldad and the bracketed nature of some glosses reflect the term's rarity and abstract quality. The -וּת ending forms a noun of quality, turning the adjective 'cruel' into the abstract concept 'cruelty.'

gloss_readable: A feminine noun meaning 'eating' or 'meal,' used in 1 Kings 19:8 where Elijah travels forty days on the strength of one meal. The definite article makes it 'the eating'—that specific consumption of bread and water provided by the angel. The term focuses on the act or occasion of eating rather than the food itself. BDB notes the nominal form's construction, deriving from the common verb אכל (to eat).

senses.1: Refers to the specific meal that sustained Elijah through his forty-day journey to Horeb. The definite article in 1 Kings 19:8 points back to the supernatural provision of verses 5-6, where an angel brought bread and water. Cross-linguistic glosses (the-eating, la-comida, le-mangeant, der-essend) vary between act and event, with Spanish comida favoring 'meal' as an event. This miraculous sustenance parallels Israel's wilderness provision, linking Elijah's prophetic mission to Mosaic foundations.

gloss_terse: and Ucal, personal name (possibly textually corrupt)
gloss_readable: A problematic name in Proverbs 30:1, where Agur addresses his oracle to Ithiel and Ucal. BDB suggests reading וָאֵכֶל ('and I am exhausted/consumed') from the root כלה instead, which would fit the context of Agur's confession of ignorance. The traditional reading as a proper name has ancient support, but the semantic awkwardness has led many scholars to propose emendation. The multilingual glosses show high uncertainty.

senses.1: Traditionally understood as the second recipient of Agur's wisdom oracle in Proverbs 30:1, though textual scholars widely suspect corruption. If personal name, Ucal joins Ithiel as addressee; if emended to וָאֵכֶל, it becomes part of Agur's self-deprecating lament ('I am weary/exhausted'). The bracketed and varied glosses (Ucal, ass, ואכל transliterated) reveal translators' discomfort. This uncertainty illustrates how ancient proper names, especially in wisdom literature's unique contexts, can preserve textual puzzles.

gloss_terse: presses, urges (of hunger driving to work)
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to press or urge, used metaphorically in Proverbs 16:26 where 'his mouth presses upon him'—that is, hunger compels the laborer to work. The Mishnaic Hebrew and Aramaic cognates support the sense of urgent pressure. The verse's parallelism shows the laboring soul working for himself, driven by the pressing demand of appetite. This root appears only here in this form, though related forms exist in post-biblical Hebrew.

senses.1: Describes hunger's compelling force that drives human labor in Proverbs 16:26. The subject 'his mouth' represents appetite or need for food, which 'presses upon him' as motivation. The parallelism ('the laboring soul labors for himself') emphasizes self-interest driven by physical necessity. This metaphorical use transforms physical pressure into existential compulsion, showing how basic needs propel human industry. The verb's rarity and the bracketed glosses suggest limited attestation, making context crucial for understanding.

gloss_terse: and my pressure, my burden (with suffix)
gloss_readable: A masculine noun with first-person suffix appearing in Job 33:7. Elihu assures Job 'my pressure/burden shall not terrify you,' promising his speech won't overwhelm. Some ancient versions (including LXX) read כַּפִּי ('my hand') instead, comparing Job 13:21, but BDB retains אַכְפִּי as related to H0404's sense of pressing. The term conveys weight of argument or force of personality that might intimidate.

senses.1: Elihu's self-reference to his rhetorical forcefulness or argumentative pressure in Job 33:7, reassuring Job he won't be overwhelmed. The first-person possessive ('my pressure') personalizes the potential burden of confrontation. While some textual traditions favor 'my hand,' the connection to אָכַף (to press, urge) supports the reading of insistent argumentation. French and German bracket the term, acknowledging textual uncertainty, while the context clearly aims to comfort: Elihu will speak as peer, not oppressor.

gloss_readable: Father of Shimei, one of Solomon's twelve district officers mentioned in 1 Kings 4:18. The name is identical to אֵלָה (terebinth tree), though whether this represents a botanical name, shortened theophoric element, or other meaning remains uncertain. Such brevity in personal names was common, and tree names often served as personal designations in ancient Israel.

senses.1: Patronymic designation identifying Shimei by his father's name in Solomon's administrative structure. In 1 Kings 4:18, Ela serves solely to distinguish this Shimei from others, functioning as genealogical marker. The multilingual transliteration (Ela) preserves the name without interpretation, though BDB's equation with אֵלָה (terebinth) suggests possible meaning. As with many biblical names appearing once, Ela's significance lies in genealogical continuity rather than narrative development.

gloss_readable: A rare verb of lamentation appearing only in Joel 1:8 as a feminine singular imperative: 'Wail like a virgin dressed in sackcloth!' The Aramaic cognates ܐܶܠܴܐ and אֲלָא support the meaning of wailing or mourning. Joel calls Judah to ritual grief over agricultural devastation. The feminine address personifies the land or community as grieving woman. Related to the interjection אַלְלַי expressing sorrow.

senses.1: Commands communal mourning over the locust plague's destruction in Joel 1:8. The feminine imperative addresses either personified Zion or the women who lead ritual lamentation. The simile 'like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth' intensifies the grief's quality—personal, raw, inconsolable. The French vers-moi and German zu-mir mistakenly read as preposition + suffix, but the Aramaic cognates confirm this as mourning terminology, echoing אַלְלַי's sorrowful cry.

gloss_readable: A feminine noun for oak or possibly terebinth tree in Joshua 24:26, where Joshua sets up a stone of witness 'under the oak which is in the sanctuary of the Lord.' The LXX translates as terebinth (τερέμινθος), and BDB suggests reading אֵלָה (terebinth) instead. Such sacred trees marked covenant sites and served as landmarks. The definite article indicates a well-known tree at Shechem's sanctuary.

senses.1: Designates the specific sacred tree at Shechem under which Joshua erected a memorial stone in Joshua 24:26. The definite article presumes readers' familiarity with this landmark tree in the Lord's sanctuary. Ancient Israelite practice often associated terebinths or oaks with sacred sites (cf. Genesis 12:6, Judges 9:6). Cross-linguistic glosses (oak, encina, chêne) maintain the arboreal reference, though botanical identification between oak and terebinth species remains debated. Such trees served as enduring witnesses to covenant commitments.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic demonstrative pronoun meaning 'these,' appearing in Jeremiah 10:11 and Ezra 5:15. Unlike Hebrew אֵלֶּה, this represents the Aramaic dialect's distinct form, used in the few Aramaic passages of the Hebrew Bible. Jeremiah 10:11's context involves pronouncing judgment on false gods: 'Thus you shall say to them: the gods who did not make heaven and earth, these shall perish.' The Aramaic insertion provides an oracle formula.

senses.1: Aramaic plural demonstrative pointing to the false gods just described in Jeremiah 10:11's judgment oracle. This linguistic code-switching—inserting an Aramaic verse into Hebrew prophecy—may reflect an international formula meant for pagan nations to understand. The form אֵלֶּה differs from standard Hebrew's expected אִלֵּין, representing dialectal variation. Multilingual glosses (these, estos, diese) preserve the deictic function, though French térébinthe appears mistaken. The Aramaic presence underscores the verse's function as direct address to idol-worshipers.

gloss_terse: and nothing, vanity (Ketiv reading, likely equals אֱלִיל)
gloss_readable: The Ketiv (written text) reading in Jeremiah 14:14, where the Qere (oral tradition) likely reads אֱלִיל (worthlessness, idol). The verse condemns prophets who prophesy 'lies, divination, worthlessness, and the deceit of their heart.' This rare form represents either a textual variant or scribal error for the more common אֱלִיל. Context clearly requires a term for falsehood or emptiness.

senses.1: Ketiv variant in Jeremiah 14:14's denunciation of false prophecy, synonymous with אֱלִיל (worthlessness, vanity). The prophet indicts those who speak from their own imagination rather than God's mouth. The bracketed nature of multilingual glosses (ketiv, nada, bracketed Hebrew) indicates textual uncertainty and probable error. Whether read as 'nothingness' or 'idol,' the sense condemns prophetic content as empty, deceptive, lacking divine origin—a recurring theme in Jeremiah's confrontation with court prophets.

gloss_readable: The name of the sixth month in the post-exilic calendar, appearing in Nehemiah 6:15 when the wall of Jerusalem was completed. Elul corresponds to August-September in modern calendars. The name derives from Akkadian Ululu and appears in Aramaic (ܐܻܝܠܘܽܠܴܐ), Arabic (أَيْلُول), and Mishnaic Hebrew. This was late summer, the month before the fall festivals of Tishri. The preposition marks temporal location.

senses.1: Temporal designation marking the completion of Jerusalem's wall reconstruction in Nehemiah 6:15, achieved remarkably in fifty-two days. The month name, borrowed from Mesopotamian calendrical tradition during the exile, shows linguistic-cultural influence on post-exilic Judean timekeeping. The preposition ל- expresses 'on/in the month of Elul,' typical Hebrew temporal syntax. Bracketed glosses suggest some translational uncertainty about proper transliteration. This late-summer timing precedes the seventh month's festivals, making the completion symbolically timely for celebration.

gloss_readable: A place name in Genesis 35:8 meaning 'oak of weeping,' where Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, was buried. The name compounds אַלּוֹן (oak) with בָּכוּת (weeping), memorializing the mourning at her death. Such commemorative naming was common in biblical geography, marking sites with events. The oak served as a natural monument, with the name preserving the community's grief across generations.

senses.1: Memorial site name preserving the location and occasion of Deborah's burial below Bethel in Genesis 35:8. The compound 'oak of weeping' combines arboreal landmark with emotional event, creating topographical memory. Ancient Israel often marked significant burials with trees (cf. Saul under tamarisk in 1 Samuel 31:13). Multilingual transliterations (Allon-Bacuth, Alon-Bakut, Allon-Bachut) preserve the Hebrew components, though meaning ('oak of weeping') makes the name self-explanatory. Such etiological names anchor sacred history in physical landscape.

gloss_terse: the Elonite (gentilic with article, descendants of Elon)
gloss_readable: The gentilic form with definite article designating members of the Elon clan within Zebulun. Numbers 26:26 uses this in the tribal census to identify descendants of Elon. The article makes it definite: 'the Elonite [family].' This follows standard Hebrew gentilic formation, adding -י suffix to the ancestor's name and often prefixing the article in genealogical contexts.

senses.1: Definite family designation for the Elonite clan within Zebulun's tribal structure in Numbers 26:26's census. The article הָ- specifies this recognized kinship group descended from Elon. Multilingual glosses (the-Elonite, los-elonitas, le-Elonite, der-Elonite) uniformly preserve definiteness, marking the clan as an established unit in Israel's tribal confederation. Such gentilics functioned administratively to organize Israel by ancestral descent, maintaining tribal identity through patrilineal genealogy.

gloss_readable: A leader from the tribe of Benjamin chosen to assist in dividing Canaan's land in Numbers 34:21. The name means 'God has loved,' combining the divine element אֵל with a form from ידד/דוד (to love). This theophoric name expresses thanksgiving for divine favor or affection. He appears only in this allocation context, representing Benjamin's interests in the land distribution.

senses.1: Tribal representative of Benjamin appointed to the land-division commission in Numbers 34:21. The name 'God has loved' reflects Israelite onomastic piety, acknowledging divine covenant faithfulness. As one of the leaders tasked with fairly apportioning Canaan among the tribes, Elidad bore significant administrative and spiritual responsibility. Multilingual transliterations uniformly preserve the name, standard practice for proper nouns. His single biblical appearance leaves no narrative beyond this crucial role in establishing tribal territories.

gloss_terse: Elihoreph, personal name (autumn God or God of harvest time)
gloss_readable: One of Solomon's two scribes mentioned in 1 Kings 4:3. The name's meaning is debated; BDB suggests 'Autumn God' (comparing Job 29:4 where חֹרֶף appears), though this remains uncertain. As a royal scribe, Elihoreph held a position of literacy and administrative power in Solomon's bureaucracy. The theophoric element אֱלִי- ('my God') was common in Israelite names.

senses.1: Royal scribe serving in Solomon's administrative cabinet in 1 Kings 4:3. The name's theophoric element ('my God') combined with חֹרֶף (autumn/harvest) may express divine providence through seasonal provision. Scribes wielded considerable influence, managing correspondence, records, and royal decrees. Multilingual transliteration (Elihoreph, Elijóref) preserves the name without interpretation. His partnership with Ahijah suggests dual secretarial roles, perhaps dividing responsibilities for Solomon's expanding kingdom and international dealings.

gloss_terse: and Elienai, personal name (variant spelling with conjunction)
gloss_readable: A Benjamite name appearing in 1 Chronicles 8:20, spelled here as אֶלְיוֹעֵנַי with conjunction. The name means 'to the Lord are my eyes' or 'my eyes are toward God,' expressing devotional orientation. Various spellings occur across Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah for different individuals, showing orthographic flexibility. This particular instance adds the conjunctive waw, typical in genealogical lists enumerating multiple sons.

senses.1: Benjamite listed among the sons of Shashak in 1 Chronicles 8:20's genealogy. The conjunction 'and' integrates Elienai into the sequential enumeration of family members. The name's meaning ('toward the Lord are my eyes') reflects piety focused on God, a common theological theme in Hebrew names. Bracketed glosses indicate transliteration challenges with this variant spelling. The Chronicler's extensive genealogies preserve tribal memory, with names like Elienai testifying to covenant faithfulness across generations.

gloss_readable: One of David's mighty warriors mentioned in 1 Chronicles 11:35, though the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 23:34 reads Eliphelet instead, suggesting textual variation. The name means 'God has judged,' from אֵל (God) and פלל (to judge/intervene). Such discrepancies between Samuel and Chronicles are common, reflecting different textual traditions or scribal variations.

senses.1: Warrior in David's elite corps of mighty men according to 1 Chronicles 11:35. The name 'God has judged' invokes divine justice or intervention, appropriate for a warrior dependent on God's favor in battle. The textual variant with 2 Samuel 23:34 (Eliphelet) shows how personal names could shift in transmission, possibly through phonetic similarity or scribal confusion. Bracketed glosses acknowledge the name's uncertain textual standing. Nevertheless, the honor of inclusion among David's champions testifies to Eliphal's valor.

gloss_readable: One of David's thirty mighty men, specifically identified as 'the Harodite' in 2 Samuel 23:25. Notably, he doesn't appear in the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11:27, suggesting either textual loss or that this represents an alternate name. The etymology of Elika is uncertain; it may be a shortened form of a longer theophoric name. His designation 'the Harodite' links him to Harod or a family from that area.

senses.1: Elite warrior among David's thirty champions in 2 Samuel 23:25, distinguished by his origin as 'the Harodite.' The name's meaning remains obscure, possibly abbreviated from a longer form. His absence from Chronicles' parallel roster raises questions about textual transmission or whether he held a brief tenure. Multilingual transliteration uniformly preserves Elika. As with many of the thirty, Scripture records only name and designation, leaving military exploits to imagination, though inclusion in this select group testifies to extraordinary courage and loyalty to David.

gloss_terse: Elisheba, personal name (God is an oath/my God is abundance)
gloss_readable: Aaron's wife, mentioned in Exodus 6:23 as daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon. The name means either 'God is an oath' (connecting to swearing) or 'my God is seven/abundance.' She bore Aaron four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The Greek Ἐλεισαβεθ (Elizabeth) derives from this name, appearing in Luke 1:5 as the mother of John the Baptist.

senses.1: Matriarch of the Aaronic priesthood, wife of Israel's first high priest in Exodus 6:23. Her name 'God is oath' or 'God is abundance' reflects covenant theology, connecting divine faithfulness to sworn promises. As mother of the priestly line, Elisheba's significance extends beyond her single mention, establishing the genealogical foundation for Israel's cultic leadership. Her descent from Judah's line (Nahshon was a prince of Judah) united priestly and royal tribal connections. The name's survival into New Testament Greek (Elizabeth) demonstrates its enduring resonance.

gloss_readable: A military captain who joined Jehoiada's conspiracy to overthrow Queen Athaliah and crown young Joash in 2 Chronicles 23:1. The name means 'God has judged,' from אֵל (God) and שׁפט (to judge). Phoenician parallels like בעלשפט and שפטבעל show the widespread use of judicial theophoric elements. Elishaphat's participation in the coup demonstrated commitment to Davidic covenant and opposition to Baal-worshiping tyranny.

senses.1: Military commander who allied with priest Jehoiada to restore legitimate Davidic rule in 2 Chronicles 23:1. The name 'God has judged' proves ironically fitting, as Elishaphat executed divine judgment against Athaliah's illegitimate reign. His role required courage—conspiring against a reigning monarch risked death if discovered. The Phoenician cognates suggest cultural interchange of onomastic patterns. Bracketed glosses indicate transliteration challenges. Elishaphat represents faithful officers who risked everything to preserve covenant kingship from Omride corruption.

gloss_terse: and Alammelech, place name (possibly 'oak of the king')
gloss_readable: A town in Asher's tribal territory mentioned in Joshua 19:26. The name may mean 'oak of the king' or 'the king's terebinth' (אַלַּת מֶלָךְ), though BDB notes uncertainty. The conjunction connects it in the list of Asherite cities. Like many border towns, precise identification remains uncertain. The name suggests either royal ownership or a significant tree marking the location.

senses.1: Territorial town allotted to Asher in Joshua 19:26's boundary description. If meaning 'oak of the king,' the name may indicate royal land holdings or a landmark tree associated with local governance. The conjunction integrates Alammelech into the sequential enumeration of Asher's inheritance. Multilingual transliterations (Alammelech, Alamelec) show slight orthographic variation. As with many Asherite towns in Galilee's northern reaches, archaeological identification remains tentative, though the name's preservation testifies to ancient Israel's careful territorial documentation.

gloss_readable: A rare masculine form of the adjective 'widowed,' used metaphorically of Israel in Jeremiah 51:5. The prophet declares that Israel and Judah are not widowed from their God—that is, not abandoned despite their guilt. The feminine form is more common; this masculine usage may be explained by agreement with the masculine national names Israel/Judah. The phrase reassures that God hasn't severed the covenant relationship.

senses.1: Metaphorical denial of covenant abandonment in Jeremiah 51:5. Though Israel sinned, God hasn't become their 'late husband,' leaving them as widow. The masculine form (unusual for a state often personified as feminine Zion) agrees with masculine Israel/Judah. This theological image reverses the widow metaphor often used for judgment (cf. Lamentations), here proclaiming continued divine fidelity. Bracketed glosses reflect the term's rarity and metaphorical usage. The passage offers hope amid Babylon's fall: God remains Israel's husband-protector despite their unfaithfulness.

gloss_readable: A masculine noun meaning widowhood, used figuratively of Babylon in Isaiah 47:9. The verse predicts that loss of children and widowhood will come upon Babylon suddenly despite her sorceries and enchantments. The conjunction links it with שְׁכוֹל (bereavement, loss of children), creating a double curse: childlessness and husband-loss. This reverses Babylon's confident boast 'I shall not sit as a widow' in verse 8.

senses.1: Symbolic judgment pronounced against Babylon in Isaiah 47:9, predicting her sudden desolation. The pairing with 'bereavement' intensifies the curse: Babylon will lose both children and protective spouse-power simultaneously. As a masculine noun (unusual for typically feminine widowhood), it may personify Babylon's empire or kings facing devastating loss. Bracketed glosses acknowledge rarity. This poetic justice answers Babylon's arrogant self-deification, reducing her from powerful matriarch to bereft, vulnerable widow—a reversal of status mirroring Babylon's treatment of conquered peoples.

gloss_readable: Father of two of David's mighty warriors, Jeribai and Joshaviah, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 11:46. The name means 'God is pleasantness' or 'God is delight,' from אֵל (God) and נעם (to be pleasant). This name appears only in Chronicles, not in the parallel Samuel list of David's champions. Such theophoric names expressed parental thanksgiving or theological conviction about God's character.

senses.1: Patronymic designating the father of two elite warriors in David's mighty men according to 1 Chronicles 11:46. The name 'God is pleasantness' reflects theological aesthetics—appreciating God's delightful nature. His absence from 2 Samuel's roster suggests Chronicles preserves additional genealogical detail. Bracketed glosses indicate simple transliteration practice for personal names. That two sons earned places among David's champions testifies to Elnaam's family's martial prowess and loyalty, suggesting he likely trained them in warfare and covenant faithfulness.

gloss_terse: and Elead, personal name (God has testified)
gloss_readable: An Ephraimite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:21, killed by men of Gath during a cattle raid. The name means 'God has testified' or 'God has borne witness,' from אֵל (God) and עוד (to testify). His death, along with his brother Ezer, caused their father Ephraim to mourn many days, after which the tribe came to comfort him. This tragic episode provides rare narrative detail within Chronicles' genealogies.

senses.1: Ephraimite victim of intertribal violence recorded in 1 Chronicles 7:21's genealogy. The name 'God has testified' may reflect parental faith in divine witness to covenant or birth circumstances. Elead's death during a cattle raid against Gath natives sparked extended mourning, humanizing Chronicles' typically bare genealogical lists. The conjunction 'and' links him with brother Ezer in their fatal venture. Bracketed glosses show standard transliteration. This incident reveals pre-conquest tensions between Israelite clans and Canaanite inhabitants, with deadly consequences for those who ventured beyond tribal boundaries.
